title: Functional, matrix & project structures
blurb: Tell functional, matrix and project structures apart, explain who holds authority in each, and why the organisation's governance shapes the project's.
question: A regional bank runs a branch refurbishment project. Its surveyors stay in the Property department and its IT engineers stay in Technology, but both now take work from a project manager as well as their line managers. Which structure is this, what problems should the project manager expect, and where will the project's approval rules come from?

teach.body: An organisation structure is the way authority, reporting lines and responsibilities are arranged. Every project lives inside two structures at once. The PERMANENT organisation is the functional or line organisation: lasting departments such as Finance or Engineering that run business as usual. The TEMPORARY organisation is the project organisation: a sponsor, project manager and team brought together for this change and disbanded when it ends. Plain English: the permanent organisation owns the people for good; the project borrows or recruits them for a while.

teach.h: The three structures you must know

children.label: Project
children.sub: Projectised: dedicated team under the PM

teach.caption: The difference between them is mainly WHO holds authority over people, money and priorities.

teach.h: How much authority does the PM have?
teach.caption: Read left to right: authority moves from the functional (line) manager to the project manager.

teach.body: Many organisations use a matrix because it shares scarce specialists across projects and business as usual. The price is two bosses. A line manager wants the person on operational work; the project manager wants them on the critical path. Without clear governance that conflict lands on the team member. The fixes are governance fixes: clear role descriptions, priorities agreed by the sponsor or board, resource commitments made up front, and a defined escalation route when line and project managers disagree.

Surveyors stay in Property and IT engineers stay in Technology, but both take tasks from the project manager: a matrix. When a payments outage pulls two engineers back to operations, the PM cannot simply overrule their line manager. She escalates the clash to the sponsor, who agrees a priority with the Technology director. Had the bank set up a dedicated refurbishment team (project structure), she would control those people directly, but at a higher cost.

teach.h: The organisation's governance shapes the project's
teach.body: A project does not invent its governance from scratch. The organisation's own governance approach (its policies, approval levels, gate rules, reporting cycles, assurance and structure) informs the governance used for the project. A public body with strict spending controls will impose formal gates and approval thresholds; a projectised engineering contractor will give its project managers more authority. The project manager tailors within that frame, never against it.

teach.h: Permanent, temporary, and where they overlap
teach.caption: A matrix is where the two organisations overlap: people belong to a department and work on a project at the same time.

teach.text: Classic confusion: in a WEAK matrix the functional (line) manager holds most of the authority and the PM is little more than a coordinator. In a STRONG matrix the PM holds most of it. A BALANCED matrix shares it. 'Projectised' means the project structure, where the PM has full authority over a dedicated team.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the structure and its defining feature (who staff report to).
State where authority sits: line manager, shared, or project manager.
Give one strength and one weakness linked to the scenario.
Explain a governance fix (agreed priorities, escalation route, clear roles).
Note that the organisation's governance approach frames the project's.
Permanent organisation = functional/line; temporary organisation = the project.
Functional: line managers hold authority; PM coordinates.
Matrix: dual reporting; weak, balanced or strong by where authority sits.
Project (projectised): dedicated team, PM has full authority, but costly.
The organisation's governance approach informs the project's governance.

summary: You can now describe functional, matrix and project structures, explain where authority sits in each and the strengths and weaknesses that follow. You can also explain why a project's governance is shaped by the permanent organisation it sits in.

A.q: A county council's library project uses staff who remain in their own departments under their line managers. The project manager coordinates their work but has little formal authority. Which structure is this?
options: Functional
Strong matrix
Projectised
Balanced matrix
A.why: In a functional structure people stay in their departments under line managers and the project manager has little authority, acting mainly as a coordinator.

whyNot.1: In a strong matrix the project manager holds most of the authority over shared staff.
whyNot.2: In a projectised structure the team is dedicated and reports to the project manager.
whyNot.3: A balanced matrix shares authority between line and project managers; here the PM has little.

A.q: What is the defining feature of a matrix organisation structure?
options: Staff report to one line manager only
Staff report to the PMO for all work
Staff report to the sponsor directly
Staff report to line manager and PM
A.why: A matrix combines the permanent line organisation with the temporary project organisation, so people have two reporting lines.

whyNot.0: A single line-manager reporting route describes a functional structure.
whyNot.1: A PMO supports projects; it is not the reporting line that defines a matrix.
whyNot.2: Team members do not normally report straight to the sponsor in any of the three structures.

A.q: Which of the following best describes a TEMPORARY organisation in project management?
options: The finance department that funds the work
The board of directors of the company
The project team, disbanded at closure
The HR function that employs the staff
A.why: The project organisation (sponsor, PM, team, board) is temporary: it is brought together for the change and disbanded when the project closes.

whyNot.0: Finance is a lasting department, part of the permanent organisation.
whyNot.1: The company board is permanent corporate governance, not a temporary structure.
whyNot.3: HR is a permanent function of the line organisation.

B.q: An engineering firm moves to a fully projectised structure for its biggest contracts. Which drawback is it MOST likely to meet?
options: Project managers lacking any authority
Team members facing two reporting lines
Weak focus on the project's objectives
Duplicated, under-used specialist staff
B.why: Dedicated teams for every project are costly: specialists and equipment get duplicated and can sit idle, and staff may have no home when the project ends.

whyNot.0: In a projectised structure the PM has full authority; lack of authority is a functional problem.
whyNot.1: Dual reporting is the hallmark of a matrix, not a projectised structure.
whyNot.2: Strong focus on project objectives is a strength of the projectised structure.

B.q: What most clearly distinguishes a STRONG matrix from a WEAK matrix?
options: PM has more authority than line managers
Staff have only one reporting line to follow
The line manager sets all project priorities
There is no sponsor or board for the project
B.why: Both are matrices with dual reporting; the difference is where authority sits. In a strong matrix the project manager holds most of it.

whyNot.1: Both weak and strong matrices have dual reporting lines.
whyNot.2: The line manager dominating priorities describes a weak matrix.
whyNot.3: Every project needs a sponsor, whatever the structure.

B.q: Why does an organisation's own governance approach matter when setting up a project's governance?
options: It is replaced by the project's own rules
It only applies to business-as-usual work
It frames the project's approval rules
It is only relevant to the PMO's reporting
B.why: The project's governance is informed by the organisation's: its policies, approval levels, gate rules and reporting set the frame the project tailors within.

whyNot.0: A project tailors within the organisation's governance; it does not replace it.
whyNot.1: Organisational governance applies to projects as well as business as usual.
whyNot.3: It shapes the whole project's governance, not just PMO reporting.

C.q: A shipbuilder is starting a six-year naval contract that needs a large, fully committed team and fast decisions by one accountable manager. Which structure is MOST appropriate?
options: Weak matrix
Functional
Projectised
Balanced matrix
C.why: A long, large, high-priority project justifies a dedicated team with the project manager holding full authority: a projectised structure.

whyNot.0: A weak matrix leaves authority with line managers, slowing decisions.
whyNot.1: A functional structure keeps people in departments, with little PM authority.
whyNot.3: A balanced matrix shares authority, which does not give one accountable manager fast control.

C.q: In a matrix organisation, a line manager keeps pulling a shared analyst back to operational work, and the project's critical path is slipping. What is the MOST appropriate response by the project manager?
options: Instruct the analyst to ignore the line manager
Escalate so the sponsor agrees the priority
Hire a contractor without telling the sponsor
Accept the delay and replan without telling anyone
C.why: In a matrix the PM cannot simply overrule the line manager. Conflicting priorities over shared staff are resolved through governance: escalation to the sponsor or board, who agree the priority.

whyNot.0: This puts the team member in an impossible position and ignores the line manager's authority.
whyNot.2: Committing spend without the sponsor bypasses governance and may exceed delegated authority.
whyNot.3: A slipping critical path must be reported; hiding it removes the sponsor's chance to decide.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT usually a strength of a functional structure?
options: Deep pools of specialist expertise
Clear career paths for specialists
Fast cross-department priority calls
Stable homes for staff after projects
C.why: Functional structures are poor at cross-functional work: each department sets its own priorities, so decisions that cut across departments are slow.

whyNot.0: Grouping specialists together builds deep expertise: a genuine strength.
whyNot.1: Specialists progress within their department: a genuine strength.
whyNot.3: Staff never leave their department, so there is no 'where next' problem: a genuine strength.

reteach.title: Putting on a school musical
reteach.question: A school puts on its summer musical using teachers who still have their normal classes. Who is in charge of whom, and how could the school organise it differently?

blocks.h: Three ways to run the show
blocks.body: Functional: each department does its bit (Music trains the band, Art paints sets) and the director can only ask nicely. Matrix: teachers stay in their departments but also take direction from the show's director, so the head of Music and the director both want Mr Patel's Thursday evenings. Project: the school hires a full-time production team who answer only to the director until the curtain falls, then leave.

steps.label: Matrix
steps.sub: Teachers answer to both department and director

steps.label: Project
steps.sub: Dedicated crew answer to the director

blocks.text: The school's own rules still apply whichever way it chooses: safeguarding policy, budget sign-off by the bursar, the head's approval for ticket prices. That is the organisation's governance informing the project's.

explain.body: The permanent organisation is the lasting line structure of departments that runs business as usual. The temporary organisation is the project organisation, created to deliver a change and disbanded at closure. Projects always sit inside the permanent organisation.

test.q: Which statement about the permanent organisation is correct?
options: It is disbanded when the project closes
It runs business as usual indefinitely
It exists only for the life of one project
It is led by the project manager full time
test.why: The permanent (functional or line) organisation is lasting and runs business as usual.

whyNot.0: Being disbanded at closure describes the temporary project organisation.
whyNot.2: Existing for one project's life describes the temporary organisation.
whyNot.3: Line managers lead the permanent organisation; the PM leads the temporary one.

explain.body: People are grouped by specialism under line managers, who control their time, budgets and priorities. The project manager mainly coordinates. Good for expertise and careers; poor for work that cuts across departments.

explain.caption: The project's work is spread across departments; no one below the top controls it all.

test.q: In a functional structure, who normally controls a team member's priorities?
options: The project manager
The product owner
The PMO lead
The line manager
test.why: In a functional structure the line (functional) manager controls staff, budgets and priorities.

whyNot.0: The PM has little authority in a functional structure.
whyNot.1: A product owner prioritises a backlog in iterative work; they do not control line priorities.
whyNot.2: A PMO supports and sets standards; it does not control individuals' priorities.

explain.body: Staff report to a line manager AND a project manager. Weak: line manager holds most authority. Balanced: authority is shared. Strong: the PM holds most. Flexible use of people, but dual reporting causes conflict over priorities unless governance sets clear escalation routes.

test.q: Which problem is MOST typical of matrix structures?
options: Conflict over priorities for shared staff
Specialists duplicated across every team
No route for staff after the project ends
Project managers with full authority
test.why: Dual reporting means line and project managers can make competing demands on the same person.

whyNot.1: Duplication of specialists is a projectised weakness.
whyNot.2: In a matrix staff simply return to their department; the 'where next' problem is projectised.
whyNot.3: Full PM authority describes the project structure, not a matrix.

explain.body: A dedicated team reports to the project manager, who has full authority over its people and budget. Strong focus and fast decisions, but costly, with duplicated specialists and the question of where people go when it ends. Whatever the structure, the organisation's governance still frames the project's.

test.q: A firm is choosing a projectised structure. Which benefit should it expect?
options: Lower cost through sharing specialists
Clear PM authority and strong focus
Easier careers inside one department
Less need for the firm's governance
test.why: A dedicated team under a PM with full authority gives clear accountability, strong focus and fast decisions.

whyNot.0: Sharing specialists is a matrix strength; projectised teams cost more.
whyNot.2: Career paths inside one department are a functional strength.
whyNot.3: The organisation's governance still informs the project's, whatever the structure.
